phy_ocra.9.0.summary: When a **current-carrying conductor** is placed in a **magnetic field**, the magnetic field of the current **interacts** with the field of the magnet and the conductor experiences a **force**: this is the **motor effect**. The direction of the force is found with **Fleming's left-hand rule**, which shows that force, current and field are all at **right angles** to each other, and reversing either the current or the field reverses the force. For a conductor at right angles to a field, the size of the force is given by **F = BIl**, where B is the **magnetic flux density** in tesla, I is the current in amps and l is the length of conductor in the field in metres.

core.p: A wire carrying a current has its own magnetic field. When that wire is placed in the field of a magnet, the two fields **interact** and the wire and the magnet **exert a force on each other**. This is called the **motor effect**.
bullets: The force only acts while a **current is flowing** in the conductor.
The force is biggest when the conductor is at **right angles (90 degrees)** to the magnetic field lines.
If the conductor is **parallel** to the field lines there is **no force**.
By **Newton's third law** the magnet experiences an **equal and opposite force** to the force on the wire.
The motor effect is the basis of **electric motors** and **loudspeakers**.

callouts.p: When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet and the conductor exert a force on each other.
There is no force without a current, and no force if the wire runs parallel to the field.

core.h: Why there is a force: interacting fields
core.p: The force is explained by the way the circular field of the wire **combines** with the uniform field of the magnet.
bullets: The current produces **circular field lines** around the wire.
On one side of the wire these circles point the **same way** as the magnet's field, so the fields **add** and the combined field is **stronger**.
On the other side they point the **opposite way**, so the fields partly **cancel** and the combined field is **weaker**.
The wire is pushed **from the stronger field towards the weaker field**.
This combined pattern is sometimes called a **catapult field**, because the stretched field lines act like a catapult flicking the wire sideways.

callouts.p: Say: the field of the current interacts with the field of the magnet; the field is strengthened on one side and weakened on the other; the wire moves towards the weaker field.

core.p: A simple practical shows the force directly.
bullets: Place a short piece of bare copper wire (or a light rod on two rails) between the poles of a **horseshoe (U-shaped) magnet**, at right angles to the field.
Connect it to a low-voltage d.c. supply with a switch.
Close the switch: the wire **jumps** or rolls along the rails, showing a force.
**Reverse the current**: the wire moves the **opposite way**.
**Turn the magnet over** (reverse the field): the wire also moves the opposite way.
Reverse **both** the current and the field: the force is in the **original direction**.
Increase the current or use a stronger magnet: the wire moves **more strongly**.
Safety: use low voltage and switch off quickly, because bare wire carrying a large current gets hot.

callouts.p: Reversing both the current and the field brings the force back to its original direction: the two reversals cancel.

core.p: **Fleming's left-hand rule** shows the relative directions of the **force**, the **current** and the **magnetic field**. All three are at right angles to each other.
bullets: Hold the **thumb, first finger and second finger** of your **left hand** at right angles to each other.
**First finger** = **Field** direction (north to south).
**seCond finger** = **Current** direction (conventional current, positive to negative).
**thuMb** = **Motion** (the direction of the **force** on the conductor).
Point the first finger along the field and the second finger along the current: the thumb shows the force.
Memory aid: **F**irst = **F**ield, se**C**ond = **C**urrent, thu**M**b = **M**otion.

callouts.t: Left hand for the motor effect
callouts.p: Use your LEFT hand for the force on a current-carrying wire (motors). The right-hand grip rule is only for finding the field around a wire.
The field always points from N to S. Getting this backwards gives the wrong force direction.

core.h: Using the left-hand rule with end-on diagrams
core.p: Exam diagrams often show the wire end-on, using dots and crosses.
bullets: A **cross** means current going **into the page**; a **dot** means current coming **out of the page**.
Example: field from left to right (N on left, S on right) and current into the page: the force is **downwards** in the plane of the page.
With the same field and current out of the page, the force is **upwards**.
Check your answer with the interacting-fields idea: the wire moves towards the side where the fields cancel.
Practise physically turning your hand: twist your wrist rather than guessing.

callouts.t: Point the second finger into the page
callouts.p: For a cross, point your second finger away from you into the paper, line the first finger up from N to S, then read off the thumb.

core.h: Factors affecting the size of the force
core.p: The size of the force on a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field depends on three quantities.
bullets: The **magnetic flux density B** (how strong the magnetic field is): stronger field, bigger force.
The **current I** in the conductor: bigger current, bigger force.
The **length l** of conductor **inside the field**: longer length in the field, bigger force.
The force is **directly proportional** to each of these: doubling any one of them doubles the force.
The **angle** matters too: maximum force at 90 degrees, zero when parallel. At GCSE, F = BIl is used only for the conductor at right angles to the field.

callouts.t: F is proportional to B, I and l
callouts.p: Double the flux density, the current or the length in the field and the force doubles.

core.p: For a conductor at right angles to a uniform magnetic field: **force = magnetic flux density x current x length**.
bullets: **F = B x I x l**
F = force on the conductor in **newtons (N)**.
B = magnetic flux density in **tesla (T)**.
I = current in **amperes (A)**.
l = length of conductor in the field in **metres (m)**.
Rearranged: **B = F / (I x l)**, **I = F / (B x l)**, **l = F / (B x I)**.

callouts.p: force on a conductor (at right angles to a magnetic field) carrying a current (N) = magnetic flux density (T) x current (A) x length (m)

callouts.t: Only the length in the field
callouts.p: Use the length of wire that is actually inside the magnetic field, not the whole length of the wire.

core.h: Magnetic flux density and the tesla
core.p: **Magnetic flux density**, B, is the measure of the **strength of a magnetic field**. Its unit is the **tesla (T)**.
bullets: A bigger flux density means the field lines are **closer together** and the force on a current is bigger.
From F = BIl, B = F / (I l), so **1 T is the flux density that gives a force of 1 N on a 1 m wire carrying 1 A** at right angles to the field.
So 1 T = 1 N/(A m).
Typical values: school bar or horseshoe magnets about 0.01 T to 0.1 T (tens of millitesla); 1 mT = 0.001 T.
In a uniform field, B is the same everywhere.

callouts.p: A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).

core.p: Marks are often lost on units rather than physics. Convert everything to N, T, A and m before substituting.
bullets: Lengths in cm: divide by 100 (5 cm = 0.05 m). Lengths in mm: divide by 1000.
Flux density in mT: divide by 1000 (40 mT = 0.040 T).
Currents in mA: divide by 1000 (250 mA = 0.25 A).
Forces in mN: divide by 1000 to get N.
Write the equation, substitute with units, then give the answer with the unit and a sensible number of significant figures.
Check with proportional reasoning: if the current triples, the force should triple.

callouts.p: Rearrange the equation before substituting numbers; it reduces arithmetic slips.

core.p: The motor effect turns electrical energy into kinetic energy in many devices.
bullets: **Electric motors**: forces on the two sides of a current-carrying coil in a field act in opposite directions, making the coil turn.
**Loudspeakers**: a changing current in a coil in a magnetic field produces a changing force that makes a cone vibrate.
**Moving-coil meters**: the force on a coil makes a pointer move.
In each, a bigger current or stronger field gives a bigger force.

analogy.t: A catapult made of field lines
analogy.p: Imagine the magnet's field lines as stretched elastic bands running from N to S. Put a current-carrying wire among them and its circular field bunches the bands up on one side and thins them out on the other. The crowded, stretched bands push the wire towards the thinner side, like a stone flung from a catapult. More current or a stronger magnet means tighter bands and a bigger push. Where it breaks down: field lines are not real elastic objects, they are a model; the force appears instantly without any stretching delay; and an elastic band pulls along its length, while the motor force acts at right angles to both the field and the current.

terms.d: The force exerted on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field (and the equal and opposite force on the magnet).
A material, such as a copper wire, that allows an electric current to flow through it.
The region around a magnet or current where a force acts on a magnet, magnetic material or current.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).
The unit of magnetic flux density; 1 T gives a force of 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field.
First finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force (motion), all at right angles, used to find the direction of the force in the motor effect.
The direction of current flow from positive to negative.
Force (N) = magnetic flux density (T) x current (A) x length of conductor in the field (m), for a conductor at right angles to the field.
A magnetic field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by parallel equally spaced lines.
The combined field pattern of a magnet and a current-carrying wire, strong on one side and weak on the other, which pushes the wire sideways.
At 90 degrees; force, current and field are mutually at right angles in the motor effect.
When one quantity doubles, the other doubles; F is directly proportional to B, I and l.
When two objects interact they exert equal and opposite forces on each other; the magnet feels a force equal and opposite to that on the wire.

mistakes.w: Using the right hand to find the direction of the force on a wire.
mistakes.r: Use Fleming's LEFT-hand rule for the motor effect.

mistakes.w: First finger = current, second finger = field.
mistakes.r: First finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force (motion).

mistakes.w: The force is greatest when the wire is parallel to the field.
mistakes.r: The force is greatest at right angles to the field and zero when the wire is parallel.

mistakes.w: Field lines point from S to N.
mistakes.r: Field lines point from N to S; use this for the first finger.

mistakes.w: Substituting a length of 5 into F = BIl when the wire is 5 cm.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres first: 5 cm = 0.05 m.

mistakes.w: Using the whole length of the wire in F = BIl.
mistakes.r: Use only the length of wire inside the magnetic field.

mistakes.w: Reversing both the current and the field reverses the force.
mistakes.r: Reversing both leaves the force in the original direction.

mistakes.w: Magnetic flux density is measured in newtons or webers.
mistakes.r: Magnetic flux density is measured in tesla (T).

mistakes.w: The force happens because the wire is a magnetic material.
mistakes.r: The force is due to the interaction between the magnetic field of the current and the field of the magnet; copper is not magnetic.

exam.q: State the name of the effect when a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force.
model: The motor effect.
exam.tip: One word answers like 'magnetism' score nothing.

exam.q: State the unit of magnetic flux density.
model: Tesla (T).
exam.tip: Learn the units of every quantity in F = BIl.

exam.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the second finger represent?
model: The (conventional) current.
exam.tip: First = Field, seCond = Current, thuMb = Motion.

exam.q: Give two ways of reversing the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.
model: Reverse the direction of the current.
Reverse the direction of the magnetic field (swap the poles).
exam.tip: Do not say 'reverse both': that leaves the force unchanged.

exam.q: Give three ways to increase the size of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.
model: Increase the current.
Use a stronger magnet / increase the magnetic flux density.
Increase the length of wire in the field.
exam.tip: These come straight from F = BIl.

exam.q: A wire 0.20 m long carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.15 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
exam.tip: Show the substitution; the unit N is needed.

exam.q: A wire 8.0 cm long carrying 2.5 A is at right angles to a magnetic field. The force on it is 0.010 N. Calculate the magnetic flux density.
exam.tip: Convert cm to m before substituting.

exam.q: A wire is placed parallel to the magnetic field lines between two magnets and a current is passed through it. State and explain what happens.
model: There is no force / the wire does not move.
The force only acts when the current has a component at right angles to the field.
exam.tip: Parallel means zero force.

exam.q: A wire is held between the poles of a magnet, with N on the left and S on the right. The current flows into the page. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on the wire.
model: First finger points left to right (N to S), second finger into the page.
The thumb points downwards: the force is downwards.
exam.tip: Turn your actual left hand and check it.

exam.q: Explain why a current-carrying wire placed between the poles of a magnet experiences a force. Describe how the direction and size of the force could be changed.
model: The current produces a (circular) magnetic field around the wire.
This field interacts with the field of the magnet.
The fields add on one side of the wire and cancel on the other, so the wire is pushed towards the weaker field.
The direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule; force, current and field are at right angles.
Reversing the current or the field reverses the force.
Increasing the current, the flux density or the length of wire in the field increases the force (F = BIl).
exam.tip: Explain the cause, then cover both direction and size.

worked.q: A copper rod of length 6.0 cm rests across two rails in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 40 mT. The current in the rod is 1.5 A and the rod is at right angles to the field. Calculate the force on the rod.
steps: Write the equation: F = B x I x l.
Convert units: B = 40 mT = 0.040 T; l = 6.0 cm = 0.060 m.
Substitute: F = 0.040 x 1.5 x 0.060.
Calculate: F = 0.0036 N.

worked.q: A wire of length 0.25 m in a field of 0.12 T experiences a force of 0.075 N when at right angles to the field. Calculate the current. Then state the force if the current is doubled and the wire is turned to lie parallel to the field.
steps: Rearrange F = BIl to I = F / (B x l).
If the current doubles and the wire stays at right angles, the force would double to 0.15 N.
But when the wire is parallel to the field there is no force, whatever the current.
worked.ans: I = 2.5 A; with the wire parallel to the field the force is 0 N.

worked.q: Field lines point from left to right and current flows out of the page. Find the direction of the force and check it using the idea of interacting fields.
steps: First finger: left to right (field). Second finger: out of the page towards you (current).
The thumb points upwards, so the force is upwards.
Check: current out of the page gives an anticlockwise field round the wire.
Below the wire, the anticlockwise circle points to the right, the same as the magnet's field, so the field is stronger below.
Above the wire it points left, opposite to the magnet's field, so the field is weaker above.
The wire is pushed from the stronger field to the weaker field: upwards.
worked.ans: The force is upwards; both methods agree.

phy_ocra.9.1.summary: An electric motor uses the **motor effect**: a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force. In a simple d.c. motor, a rectangular coil sits between the poles of a magnet; the two long sides carry current in **opposite directions**, so they are pushed in opposite directions and the coil experiences a **turning effect (moment)**. A **split-ring commutator** reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the turning effect always acts the same way and the coil keeps spinning. The speed and turning force increase with a larger current, a stronger magnetic field and more turns on the coil.

core.p: An electric motor transfers energy from the **electrical store** of a supply into the **kinetic store** of a spinning shaft. It works because a wire carrying a current inside a magnetic field experiences a force (the motor effect). Arranging wires as a coil turns these straight-line pushes into rotation.
bullets: Input: electrical work done by the current
Useful output: kinetic energy of the rotating coil and shaft
Wasted output: heating of the coil (resistance) and friction at the bearings and brushes, plus sound
Used in fans, drills, washing machines, electric cars, hard drives and toys

callouts.p: A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a **force**. Two forces in opposite directions on opposite sides of a coil produce a **turning effect** that makes the coil rotate.

core.h: Parts of a simple d.c. motor
core.p: The simple d.c. motor has a small number of parts, and you must be able to name each one and say what it does.
bullets: **Permanent magnets** (or electromagnets): provide a uniform magnetic field from N to S across the coil
**Rectangular coil** of insulated wire: carries the current; free to rotate on an axle
**Axle (shaft)**: the coil is mounted on it; it delivers the rotation to whatever the motor drives
**Split-ring commutator**: a ring cut into two halves, fixed to the coil so it turns with it; reverses the current direction in the coil every half turn
**Carbon brushes**: stationary contacts that press on the commutator and carry current between the supply and the spinning coil
**d.c. supply** (cell or battery): provides the current

head: Part
Job
rows: Carries current; forces act on its sides
Keep electrical contact while coil spins
Lets coil rotate and transfers motion

core.p: Look at the two long sides of the coil that lie at right angles to the field. Current flows along one side in one direction and back along the other side in the **opposite direction**. Using Fleming's left-hand rule, the force on one side is up and the force on the other side is down. These two forces are equal in size, opposite in direction and act along different lines, so they form a **couple** that produces a **moment** about the axle.
bullets: Forces on the two sides are equal and opposite, so there is no overall push sideways, only turning
The forces act on opposite sides of the axle, so both turn the coil the **same way** (e.g. both clockwise)
The short sides of the coil are parallel to the field when the coil is flat, so they feel no force
Direction of rotation is found with **Fleming's left-hand rule**: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion

callouts.p: For full marks link: current in coil, in a magnetic field, force on each side, forces in **opposite directions** because current is in opposite directions, so a **turning effect**.

core.h: The turning effect changes as the coil rotates
core.p: The size of the turning effect depends on the angle of the coil. The forces on the sides always point up and down (at right angles to the field and the current), but their **perpendicular distance** from the axle changes as the coil rotates.
bullets: Coil **parallel** to the field (flat): forces have the biggest perpendicular distance from the axle, so the **turning effect is maximum**
Coil **perpendicular** to the field (vertical): forces act through the axle line, so the **turning effect is zero**
The coil carries on past the vertical position because of its **momentum**
Without a commutator, once past vertical the forces would turn it back, so it would just rock and stop in the vertical position

head: Coil position
Turning effect
What happens
rows: Momentum carries it on; commutator swaps current

core.p: The commutator solves the problem of the coil stopping at the vertical position. Every **half turn**, just as the coil passes the vertical, the gaps in the split ring pass the brushes and each half of the ring swaps to the other brush. This **reverses the direction of the current in the coil**.
bullets: Reversing the current reverses the forces on each side of the coil
Because the sides have also swapped places, the side now on the left still gets pushed up and the side on the right still gets pushed down
So the turning effect is always in the **same direction** and the coil keeps rotating continuously
The current from the supply is d.c.; the commutator makes the current in the coil itself alternate in direction every half turn

callouts.p: A split metal ring attached to the coil that **reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn**, so the coil keeps turning in the same direction.
The commutator does not change the supply. It reverses the current **in the coil** every half turn. Do not say it reverses the magnetic field.

core.p: The coil spins but the wires from the battery cannot, or they would twist up. Brushes are stationary contacts that rub against the spinning commutator to keep the circuit complete.
bullets: Usually made of **carbon (graphite)**: conducts electricity and is slippery so friction is low
Pressed onto the commutator by springs
They wear down over time and need replacing
Sparking and friction at the brushes waste some energy

core.h: Making a motor turn faster or with more force
core.p: The force on each side of the coil is given by F = BIl (covered in P4.2a-c). For a coil with many turns, each turn adds its own force. So anything that increases B, I, l or the number of turns increases the turning effect, which makes the motor spin faster or able to turn a bigger load.
bullets: **Increase the current** (higher p.d. supply)
Use a **stronger magnetic field** (stronger magnets, or poles closer together)
Use **more turns of wire** on the coil
Use a **longer coil side** inside the field (bigger coil)
Wind the coil on a **soft iron core** (armature), which concentrates the magnetic field through the coil

callouts.p: More current, stronger magnet, more turns on the coil. These are the three answers mark schemes most often want.

core.p: Since the force direction depends on both the current direction and the field direction, the motor can be made to spin the other way.
bullets: **Reverse the current** (swap the battery connections), OR
**Reverse the magnetic field** (swap the magnets round)
Reversing **both** at once leaves the rotation direction unchanged
Check with Fleming's left-hand rule: flipping one finger flips the thumb

core.p: A motor is a device that transfers energy, so the ideas of useful and wasted energy and efficiency apply.
bullets: Useful: electrical store to **kinetic store** of the shaft (and then to whatever it lifts or moves)
Wasted: **thermal store** of the coil and surroundings due to resistance (current heating) and friction
efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer
Reduce waste with low-resistance thick copper wire, lubricated bearings and low-friction brushes

callouts.p: Say 'energy is transferred electrically to the kinetic store of the motor', not 'electricity turns into movement'.

core.p: Real motors improve on the simple single-loop design, but the physics is the same.
bullets: Many coils at different angles on one shaft, each with its own commutator segments, give a **smoother, steadier** turning effect (no dead spot)
Coils wound on a laminated **soft iron armature** strengthen the field
**Electromagnets** can be used instead of permanent magnets for a stronger, controllable field
Motor speed can be controlled by varying the current, for example with a variable resistor

core.h: Comparing the motor and the generator
core.p: It helps to know which way round the energy goes, even though generators belong to other spec points. In a motor, a current in a field produces motion. In a generator, motion in a field produces a current.
bullets: Motor: electrical energy in, kinetic energy out
Motor uses **Fleming's left-hand rule**
Both use coils, magnets and brushes
A d.c. motor uses a **split-ring** commutator

callouts.p: Use your **left** hand for motors. Mixing up hands gives the wrong direction of rotation.

analogy.p: Imagine two people pushing a revolving door at opposite edges, one pushing forwards and one pulling backwards. Their pushes are opposite but both make the door turn the same way, just like the up and down forces on the two sides of the coil. When the door panel points straight at them, pushing just squashes it against the spindle and nothing turns: this is the vertical position with zero turning effect. The commutator is like the two people instantly swapping roles at that moment so the door keeps going round. Where it breaks down: people push by choice, but the force on the coil comes from the interaction of the current's magnetic field with the magnet's field, and the 'swap' is the current reversing, not the forces deciding to change.

terms.d: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force.
A device that uses the motor effect to transfer energy from an electrical supply to a kinetic store by making a coil rotate.
Many turns of insulated wire, free to rotate in the magnetic field; forces act on its sides when current flows.
A split ring fixed to the coil that reverses the direction of current in the coil every half turn so it keeps rotating the same way.
Stationary carbon contacts that press against the commutator and connect the rotating coil to the supply.
The rotating effect of a force about a pivot; force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the pivot.
A pair of equal and opposite forces acting along different lines, which causes rotation but no overall sideways movement.
The shaft on which the coil turns; it carries the rotation to the load.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, in tesla (T).
First finger points along the field (N to S), second finger along the conventional current, thumb gives the direction of the force (motion).
The soft iron core on which the coil is wound; it concentrates the magnetic field and increases the turning effect.
Current that flows in one direction only, such as from a cell or battery.
Current direction taken as flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the supply.
Useful output energy transfer divided by total input energy transfer.

mistakes.w: The commutator reverses the magnetic field.
mistakes.r: The commutator reverses the direction of the **current in the coil** every half turn; the field stays the same.

mistakes.w: The commutator reverses the current every full turn.
mistakes.r: It reverses the current **every half turn**, as the coil passes the vertical position.

mistakes.w: The forces on both sides of the coil are in the same direction.
mistakes.r: The current flows in **opposite directions** in the two sides, so the forces are in **opposite directions**, producing a turning effect.

mistakes.w: The turning effect is biggest when the coil is vertical.
mistakes.r: The turning effect is **maximum when the coil is parallel to the field** and **zero when it is perpendicular** (vertical).

mistakes.w: Use a bigger battery to make it spin faster.
mistakes.r: Increase the **current** (or p.d.); 'bigger battery' is too vague to score.

mistakes.w: Brushes are made of metal wire brushes to clean the commutator.
mistakes.r: Brushes are **carbon** contacts that keep **electrical contact** with the rotating commutator.

mistakes.w: Reversing both the current and the magnets reverses the motor.
mistakes.r: Reversing both **cancels out**; the direction of rotation stays the same.

mistakes.w: Electrical energy is turned into kinetic energy.
mistakes.r: Energy is **transferred electrically** to the **kinetic store** of the coil; some is wasted to the thermal store.

mistakes.w: Use the right-hand rule to find which way the motor turns.
mistakes.r: Use **Fleming's left-hand rule** for motors.

exam.q: State the name of the part of a d.c. motor that reverses the current in the coil every half turn.
model: Split-ring commutator
exam.tip: 'Commutator' alone usually scores, but write split-ring commutator to be safe.

exam.q: State two ways of making a d.c. motor spin faster.
model: Increase the current / p.d.
Use a stronger magnet / more turns on the coil
exam.tip: Any two of: more current, stronger field, more turns, soft iron core.

exam.q: State two ways to reverse the direction of rotation of a d.c. motor.
model: Reverse the direction of the current (swap battery connections)
Reverse the magnetic field (swap the poles of the magnets)
exam.tip: Say these are alternatives; doing both cancels out.

exam.q: Explain why the coil of a motor experiences a turning effect when a current flows.
model: Current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force (motor effect)
Current flows in opposite directions in the two sides of the coil
So the forces on the two sides are in opposite directions (one up, one down)
Forces act on opposite sides of the axle, giving a moment / turning effect
exam.tip: Keep the chain of reasoning in order; each link is a mark.

exam.q: Explain why a simple motor needs a split-ring commutator.
model: Without it, after half a turn the forces would turn the coil back the other way
The commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn
So the forces always produce rotation in the same direction / coil keeps turning
exam.tip: Mention 'every half turn' and 'same direction'.

exam.q: State the job of the brushes in a motor.
model: Keep electrical contact between the supply and the rotating commutator/coil
exam.tip: Do not say they clean the commutator.

exam.q: Describe how the size of the turning effect on the coil changes as it turns from horizontal (parallel to the field) to vertical.
model: Turning effect is maximum when coil is parallel to the field
Decreases to zero when coil is perpendicular to the field (vertical)
exam.tip: Link it to the perpendicular distance of the forces from the axle.

exam.q: A student reverses both the battery and the magnets of a motor. Explain what happens to the direction of rotation.
model: Reversing either one reverses the force
Reversing both reverses the force twice, so the direction is unchanged
exam.tip: Use Fleming's left-hand rule to check.

exam.q: Describe the energy transfers in an electric motor and explain why it is not 100% efficient.
model: Energy transferred electrically to kinetic store of the coil/shaft
Some energy wasted to thermal store due to resistance of the coil (heating)
Some wasted by friction at bearings/brushes (and sound)
exam.tip: Name the stores.

exam.q: Explain in detail how a simple d.c. motor works. Include the roles of the coil, the magnets, the commutator and the brushes.
model: Magnets provide a magnetic field across the coil
Brushes connect the d.c. supply to the coil via the commutator
Current in the coil in a magnetic field gives a force on each side (motor effect)
Current is in opposite directions in the two sides, so forces are opposite, giving a turning effect
Coil rotates; momentum carries it past the vertical position
Split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn
So the turning effect is always the same way and the coil rotates continuously
Direction found by Fleming's left-hand rule
exam.tip: Level-of-response: you need a logical sequence covering all four parts for Level 3.

exam.q: Suggest why real motors use several coils set at different angles.
model: A single coil has zero turning effect when vertical
Several coils mean one is always near the maximum position, giving smoother / steadier rotation
exam.tip: The word 'smoother' is the key idea.

worked.q: One side of a motor coil has 50 turns, each 0.04 m long in the field. The field is 0.2 T and the current is 1.5 A. Calculate the total force on that side of the coil.
steps: Force on one turn: F = BIl = 0.2 x 1.5 x 0.04
F = 0.012 N per turn
50 turns each feel this force: total F = 50 x 0.012
Total F = 0.6 N
worked.ans: 0.6 N (the other side feels 0.6 N in the opposite direction, giving a turning effect).

worked.q: A motor coil is flat between N (left) and S (right). Current flows away from you in the left side and towards you in the right side. Describe the forces and the direction of rotation, viewed from the front.
steps: Field points left to right (N to S)
Left side: current into page, Fleming's left-hand rule gives force down
Right side: current out of page, force up
Left goes down, right goes up: the coil turns anticlockwise
At the vertical, the commutator reverses the current so it keeps turning anticlockwise
worked.ans: Equal and opposite forces (down on left, up on right) turn the coil anticlockwise continuously.

worked.q: A motor takes in 600 J of electrical energy and transfers 420 J to the kinetic store of a load. Calculate the efficiency and the energy wasted.
steps: efficiency = useful output / total input = 420 / 600
efficiency = 0.7 = 70%
wasted energy = 600 - 420 = 180 J, mostly to the thermal store

phy_ocra.9.2.summary: **Electromagnetic induction** (the generator effect) happens when the magnetic field through or around a conductor **changes**. This induces a **potential difference** across the ends of the conductor, and if it is part of a complete circuit an **induced current** flows. The induced current creates its own magnetic field that **opposes the change** that caused it. A bigger p.d. is induced by changing the field faster, using a stronger magnet, or using more turns of wire; reversing the change reverses the induced p.d.

core.p: If a conductor and a magnetic field move relative to each other, or the magnetic field around a conductor changes in strength, a **potential difference is induced** across the ends of the conductor. This is the reverse of the motor effect: instead of current plus field giving motion, motion (or change) plus field gives a p.d.
bullets: Also called the **generator effect**
The key word is **change**: a steady field with no movement induces nothing
A p.d. is induced even in an open circuit; a **current** flows only if the circuit is complete
Energy is transferred from the kinetic store of whatever moves (or the changing supply) to the circuit

callouts.p: A potential difference is induced across a conductor when it experiences a **change in the magnetic field** (relative movement or a change in field strength). If the circuit is complete, this p.d. drives an **induced current**.

core.p: Any situation where the magnetic field linked with a conductor changes will do. There are three common set-ups.
bullets: **Moving a magnet** into or out of a coil of wire
**Moving a wire** so that it cuts through magnetic field lines (e.g. between the poles of a magnet)
**Changing the current** in a nearby electromagnet (switching it on or off, or using a.c.), so the field through a second coil changes
Moving the coil towards a stationary magnet works just as well as moving the magnet: only **relative** movement matters

callouts.p: A straight wire must move **across** the field lines to induce a p.d. Moving it along (parallel to) the field lines induces nothing.

core.p: Connect a coil to a sensitive **centre-zero ammeter (galvanometer)** and move a bar magnet in and out. This is the classic demonstration.
bullets: Push the N pole in: needle flicks one way
Hold the magnet still inside the coil: **no reading**, because nothing is changing
Pull the N pole out: needle flicks the **opposite** way
Push the S pole in: needle flicks the opposite way to pushing N in
Move faster: bigger deflection

core.h: Factors that increase the induced p.d.
core.p: The induced p.d. depends on **how quickly** the magnetic field through the conductor changes. Anything that makes the change bigger or faster increases it.
bullets: Move the magnet or wire **faster** (greater speed of relative movement)
Use a **stronger magnet** (greater magnetic flux density)
Use **more turns** on the coil: each turn has a p.d. induced and these add up
Wind the coil on an **iron core** to concentrate the field
For a coil, a larger area of coil catches more field

callouts.p: Faster movement, stronger magnet, more turns on the coil. These earn the marks in almost every 'how could the p.d. be increased' question.

core.h: Factors that reverse the induced p.d.
core.p: The direction of the induced p.d. (and current) depends on the direction of the change.
bullets: **Reverse the direction of movement** (in instead of out)
**Reverse the magnetic field** (use the other pole of the magnet)
Doing both together gives the **same** direction as the original
In a generator that keeps turning, the direction reverses every half turn, giving alternating current

core.h: The induced current opposes the change
core.p: When an induced current flows, it creates its **own magnetic field**. This field always acts to **oppose the change** that produced it. This is the key Higher-level idea in the OCR specification.
bullets: Push a N pole towards a coil: the near end of the coil becomes a **N pole**, which repels the magnet
Pull a N pole away: the near end becomes a **S pole**, which attracts the magnet back
So you always have to **do work** to move the magnet: you feel resistance
This is why energy is conserved: the electrical energy in the circuit comes from the work you do against this opposing force

callouts.p: The induced current generates a magnetic field that **opposes the original change** (in movement or field). If it helped the change instead, you would get energy for nothing, which breaks conservation of energy.

callouts.t: Opposes the change, not the field
callouts.p: The induced field opposes the **change**, not the magnet's field itself. Pulling the magnet out gives an induced field that tries to keep it in.

core.p: Induction does not create energy. Because the induced field opposes the motion, a force must be applied to keep the magnet or wire moving.
bullets: Work done by the person or turbine = energy transferred to the circuit (plus losses)
With an open circuit (no current), there is no opposing force and it is easy to move the magnet
With a complete circuit and a large current, moving the magnet is harder
This is why a bike dynamo is harder to pedal when the lights are on

core.p: Movement is not essential. What matters is a **change in the magnetic field** through the coil. A changing current in one coil makes a changing field, which induces a p.d. in a second coil nearby.
bullets: Switching a current **on** in coil 1: brief p.d. induced in coil 2
Current steady: **no** induced p.d. (field is not changing)
Switching **off**: brief p.d. in the opposite direction
Using **alternating current** in coil 1 gives a constantly changing field, so an alternating p.d. is induced continuously in coil 2 (the principle behind transformers)

core.h: Comparing motor effect and generator effect
core.p: Students often confuse the two effects. They are opposite processes.
bullets: Motor effect: current + field gives a **force/motion**
Generator effect: motion (change) + field gives an **induced p.d./current**
Both rely on the interaction between magnetic fields
The opposing force from an induced current is itself a motor effect force

core.p: Exams often show a graph of induced p.d. against time, for example as a magnet falls through a coil.
bullets: As the magnet enters the coil, a p.d. pulse appears in one direction
While the magnet is passing through the middle, the change is small, so the p.d. is near zero
As it leaves, a pulse in the **opposite** direction appears
The second pulse is **taller and narrower** because the magnet is falling faster as it leaves (faster change)
Area under each pulse is about the same

callouts.p: Faster movement gives a larger peak p.d. but for a shorter time.

core.p: This effect underpins the generation and distribution of almost all mains electricity, and several everyday devices.
bullets: Generators in power stations (alternators) and bicycle dynamos
Transformers in the National Grid
Microphones (sound waves move a coil in a magnetic field)
Induction hobs and wireless chargers

analogy.t: A door that resists being moved
analogy.p: Think of the coil as a stubborn door closer that resists any change. If you push the door open, the closer pushes back; if you try to slam it shut, the closer slows it down. A coil does the same with magnetic field: push a magnet in and the induced current pushes it back out; pull it away and the induced current tries to hold on to it. The faster you try to change things, the harder it resists, just as a faster change gives a bigger induced p.d. Where it breaks down: a door closer resists even when you hold the door still, but a coil only responds while the field is changing; with no change there is no induced current and no opposing force.

terms.d: The induction of a potential difference across a conductor when the magnetic field around it changes.
Another name for electromagnetic induction: movement or a changing field produces a p.d.
The p.d. produced across a conductor by a changing magnetic field.
The current that flows when an induced p.d. acts in a complete circuit.
Movement of the magnet and conductor with respect to each other; either can move.
Lines showing the direction of force on a north pole, running from N to S outside a magnet.
Moving a conductor across a magnetic field so it passes through field lines, inducing a p.d.
Many turns of wire; the p.d. induced in each turn adds, increasing the total.
A sensitive centre-zero ammeter that shows the size and direction of a small current.
The strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).
The induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the change that caused it.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred; work must be done to induce a current.
An easily magnetised core that concentrates the magnetic field through a coil.

mistakes.w: A magnet held still inside a coil induces a current.
mistakes.r: A p.d. is induced only when the field is **changing**; a stationary magnet induces nothing.

mistakes.w: The induced current helps the magnet move into the coil.
mistakes.r: The induced current's field **opposes the change**, so it repels the approaching magnet.

mistakes.w: Use a bigger magnet.
mistakes.r: Use a **stronger** magnet; size is not the same as field strength.

mistakes.w: A current is always induced when a wire moves in a field.
mistakes.r: A **p.d.** is induced; a current only flows if the circuit is **complete**.

mistakes.w: Moving the wire along the field lines induces a p.d.
mistakes.r: The wire must move **across** (cut) the field lines.

mistakes.w: Induction creates energy.
mistakes.r: Work is done against the opposing force; energy is **transferred**, not created.

mistakes.w: Reversing both the magnet and the direction of motion reverses the current.
mistakes.r: Reversing both gives the **same** direction as before.

mistakes.w: The induced field opposes the magnet's field.
mistakes.r: It opposes the **change** in field: when the magnet is pulled out, the induced field tries to keep the field there.

exam.q: State what is meant by electromagnetic induction.
model: A potential difference is induced across a conductor
when the magnetic field around it changes / when it moves relative to a magnetic field
exam.tip: Say 'potential difference', not just 'electricity'.

exam.q: A magnet is held at rest inside a coil connected to an ammeter. State and explain the ammeter reading.
model: Zero
No change in magnetic field / no relative movement, so no p.d. induced
exam.tip: Always link to 'change'.

exam.q: Give three ways to increase the p.d. induced when a magnet is moved into a coil.
model: Move the magnet faster
Use a stronger magnet
Use more turns on the coil
exam.tip: An iron core also scores on most schemes.

exam.q: State two ways of reversing the direction of the induced current.
model: Move the magnet in the opposite direction (out instead of in)
Turn the magnet round / use the other pole
exam.tip: Do not give both together as one method; that cancels.

exam.q: The N pole of a magnet is pushed into a coil in a complete circuit. State the polarity of the end of the coil nearest the magnet and explain why.
model: North pole
The induced current creates a magnetic field that opposes the change
A N pole repels the approaching N pole / opposes the magnet moving in
exam.tip: Higher tier: always mention 'opposes the change'.

exam.q: Explain why it is harder to move a magnet into a coil when the coil is connected to a complete circuit than when the circuit is broken.
model: In a complete circuit an induced current flows
The current produces a magnetic field that opposes the motion of the magnet
So work must be done against this force; with a broken circuit there is no current and no opposing force
exam.tip: Link to energy conservation for extra clarity.

exam.q: A wire is moved parallel to the magnetic field lines between two poles. State and explain whether a p.d. is induced.
model: No p.d. induced
The wire does not cut field lines / no change in field linked with the wire
exam.tip: Movement must be across the field.

exam.q: A magnet is dropped through a coil connected to a data logger. Describe and explain the shape of the p.d.-time graph.
model: A pulse of p.d. as the magnet enters the coil
Near-zero p.d. while it is inside / in the middle
A pulse in the opposite direction as it leaves
The second pulse is larger (and shorter) because the magnet is moving faster
exam.tip: Opposite direction because the change reverses (field increasing then decreasing).

exam.q: Two coils are wound on the same iron core. Coil 1 is connected to a d.c. supply and a switch. Describe what a meter connected to coil 2 shows when the switch is closed, left closed and then opened.
model: Brief deflection when switch closed (field increasing)
Zero while current is steady (no change)
Brief deflection in the opposite direction when opened (field decreasing)
exam.tip: No movement is needed; a changing current gives a changing field.

exam.q: Explain in detail how a p.d. can be induced in a coil, what affects its size and direction, and why the induced current makes it harder to move the magnet.
model: Relative movement of magnet and coil / changing field through coil induces a p.d.
Current flows if the circuit is complete
Larger p.d. with faster movement
Larger p.d. with stronger magnet / more turns / iron core
Direction reverses if motion or pole reversed
Induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the change
So work must be done to move the magnet; energy is transferred to the circuit
exam.tip: Structure: cause, size, direction, opposition/energy.

worked.q: A student pushes the N pole of a magnet into a coil and the meter needle moves 4 divisions to the right. Predict the reading when she (a) pulls the N pole out at the same speed, (b) pushes the S pole in twice as fast.
steps: (a) Reversing the direction of movement reverses the induced p.d.
Same speed gives the same size: 4 divisions to the left
(b) Using the S pole reverses the direction: needle moves left
Moving twice as fast makes the field change twice as quickly, so a larger deflection, about 8 divisions
worked.ans: (a) 4 divisions left; (b) larger deflection (about 8 divisions) to the left.

worked.q: Explain, using the idea of opposing the change, which way a coil's near end is magnetised as a S pole is pulled away from it.
steps: The change is a S pole moving away
To oppose this, the coil tries to keep the magnet near: it must attract it
Opposite poles attract, so the near end of the coil becomes a N pole
worked.ans: The near end becomes a N pole, attracting the retreating S pole.

phy_ocra.9.3.summary: Generators use **electromagnetic induction**: a coil is rotated in a magnetic field, so the field through the coil keeps changing and a **potential difference is induced**. An **alternator** (a.c. generator) connects the coil to the circuit through **slip rings and brushes**, so the output reverses direction every half turn and is **alternating current**. A **dynamo** (d.c. generator) uses a **split-ring commutator** instead, which swaps the connections every half turn so the output always flows the **same way (direct current)**. Turning the coil faster gives a larger peak p.d. and, for an alternator, a higher frequency.

core.p: A generator transfers energy from the **kinetic store** of a rotating shaft (turned by a turbine, engine, wind or a bicycle wheel) to an **electrical** output. It is the reverse of a motor: motion in a magnetic field gives an induced p.d. and current.
bullets: Based on the **generator effect** (electromagnetic induction)
A coil rotates in a magnetic field, or a magnet rotates inside fixed coils
As it turns, the magnetic field through the coil **continuously changes**, so a p.d. is continuously induced
Work must be done to turn it, because the induced current's field **opposes the motion**

callouts.p: **Alternator** = a.c. generator with **slip rings**. **Dynamo** = d.c. generator with a **split-ring commutator**.

core.p: A simple alternator looks like a d.c. motor, but the coil connects to the outside circuit through two complete rings instead of a split ring.
bullets: **Magnets**: provide the magnetic field
**Coil** of wire on an axle, turned by an external force
**Slip rings**: two separate complete rings, each permanently joined to one end of the coil, turning with it
**Brushes**: stationary carbon contacts pressing on each slip ring, connecting the coil to the external circuit
Each brush is always connected to the **same end** of the coil

callouts.p: Two complete conducting rings, each connected to one end of the rotating coil, which keep the coil connected to the external circuit **without reversing the connections**, so the output is a.c.

core.p: As the coil rotates, each side moves up through the field for half a turn and then down through it for the next half turn. Reversing the direction of movement reverses the induced p.d. Since the slip rings never swap the connections, the output to the circuit also reverses every half turn.
bullets: Side A moves up then down; the induced p.d. in it reverses every **half turn**
Slip rings keep each end of the coil joined to the same brush
So the current in the external circuit changes direction every half turn: **alternating current**
One full rotation of the coil gives **one complete cycle** of a.c.

core.h: When the p.d. is biggest and smallest
core.p: The size of the induced p.d. depends on how quickly the sides of the coil are **cutting field lines**, which depends on the coil's angle.
bullets: Coil plane **parallel** to the field: sides move straight across the field lines, cutting them fastest, so the induced p.d. is **maximum (peak)**
Coil plane **perpendicular** to the field: sides move along the field lines momentarily, cutting none, so the induced p.d. is **zero**
This happens twice per rotation, so the p.d. passes through zero twice each turn
The output varies smoothly, giving a **sine-shaped** p.d.-time graph

callouts.t: Do not mix this up with the motor
callouts.p: Use the coil's angle to the field, not words like 'horizontal', since the magnets could be placed either way. Peak p.d. occurs when the coil plane is **parallel** to the field.

core.p: A graph of p.d. against time for an alternator is a wave that goes positive and negative.
bullets: Positive half: current one way; negative half: current the other way
The height of each peak is the **peak p.d.**
The time for one complete wave is the **period** T, equal to the time for one rotation
frequency f = 1 / T, measured in hertz (Hz); UK mains is **50 Hz**, so power station generators complete 50 cycles each second

core.h: Parts and action of a dynamo
core.p: A dynamo produces direct current. It is built like an alternator but uses a **split-ring commutator**, exactly as in a d.c. motor, instead of slip rings.
bullets: The commutator is a single ring split into two halves, each half joined to one end of the coil
Every **half turn**, just as the induced p.d. in the coil reverses, the commutator halves swap brushes
So the connections to the external circuit swap at the same moment the p.d. in the coil reverses
The two reversals cancel, so the current in the external circuit always flows in the **same direction**

callouts.p: A generator that uses a **split-ring commutator** to reverse the connections to the coil every half turn, so its output is **direct current**.

core.p: The dynamo's p.d.-time graph looks like the a.c. wave with all the negative halves flipped up above the axis.
bullets: The p.d. is always **positive**: one direction only
It still **varies** in size, rising to a peak and falling to zero twice every rotation
Zeros occur when the coil plane is perpendicular to the field, the instant the commutator swaps
Called **d.c.** because it never changes direction, even though it is not steady like a battery

callouts.p: For a dynamo, draw a row of humps that all touch the time axis and never go below it. Same peak height and same time per hump as the a.c. graph from the same coil.

core.p: The only design difference is the type of rings, but it changes the output completely.
bullets: Alternator: slip rings, a.c. output
Dynamo: split-ring commutator, d.c. output
Both: rotating coil, magnetic field, brushes, induced p.d.
Both need work to be done to keep them turning

core.p: The induced p.d. depends on how quickly the magnetic field through the coil changes, so anything that speeds up or strengthens the change increases the output.
bullets: **Rotate the coil faster**: larger peak p.d. AND (for an alternator) higher frequency, because each cycle takes less time
Use a **stronger magnetic field** (stronger magnets or electromagnets): larger peak p.d., same frequency
Use **more turns** on the coil: larger peak p.d., same frequency
Use an **iron core** to concentrate the field
Larger area of coil

callouts.p: Turning faster makes the peaks **taller** and **closer together**. Stronger magnets or more turns only make them taller.

core.p: Large power station alternators work on the same principle, with some practical differences.
bullets: Often an **electromagnet rotates** inside fixed coils, so the large output current does not need to pass through sliding contacts
The rotor is turned by a turbine driven by steam, water or wind
They rotate to give a frequency of 50 Hz for the UK National Grid
Car alternators charge the battery after the a.c. is converted to d.c.

core.p: When a generator supplies a current, the current in the coil experiences a motor effect force that opposes the rotation. This is why energy is conserved.
bullets: Larger current drawn means a larger opposing force, so more work is needed to keep it turning
Example: a bicycle dynamo is harder to pedal when the lamp is switched on
With no load (open circuit), there is a p.d. but no current and it turns easily
Energy transfer: kinetic store of the rotor to electrical, with some wasted as heating and sound

analogy.t: A Ferris wheel and a traffic officer
analogy.p: Picture each side of the coil as a person going round on a Ferris wheel: half the time they are rising, half the time falling, so the 'push' they create reverses every half turn. With slip rings, the wheel's riders are always plugged into the same side of the road, so traffic flows one way then the other: a.c. With a commutator, a traffic officer swaps the lanes at the exact moment the riders change from rising to falling, so the cars on the road always go the same way: d.c. Where it breaks down: riders do not generate anything themselves; the p.d. comes from the coil cutting magnetic field lines, and its size also depends on how steeply the sides are crossing the field, not just whether they are going up or down.

terms.d: A device that transfers energy from a kinetic store to an electrical output using electromagnetic induction.
An a.c. generator: a coil rotating in a magnetic field connected through slip rings.
A d.c. generator: a coil rotating in a magnetic field connected through a split-ring commutator.
Two complete rings, each joined to one end of the coil, so the connections never swap and the output alternates.
A split ring that swaps the coil's connections every half turn, giving a d.c. output.
Stationary carbon contacts that connect the rotating rings to the external circuit.
Current that repeatedly reverses its direction.
Current that flows in one direction only.
The maximum value of the induced potential difference in each cycle.
The time for one complete cycle; for a simple generator, the time for one rotation.
The number of complete cycles per second, in hertz (Hz); f = 1 / T.
The induction of a p.d. across a conductor when the magnetic field around it changes.
A conductor moving across a magnetic field; the faster it cuts lines, the larger the induced p.d.
The rotating part of a generator (coil or electromagnet).

mistakes.w: A dynamo produces a.c. and an alternator produces d.c.
mistakes.r: Alternator = **a.c.** (slip rings); dynamo = **d.c.** (split-ring commutator).

mistakes.w: Spinning faster only makes the peaks taller.
mistakes.r: Faster rotation increases the **peak p.d. and the frequency**.

mistakes.w: Using stronger magnets increases the frequency.
mistakes.r: Stronger magnets increase the **peak p.d. only**; frequency depends on rotation speed.

mistakes.w: The p.d. is biggest when the coil is perpendicular to the field.
mistakes.r: The p.d. is **maximum when the coil plane is parallel to the field** (sides cutting field lines fastest) and zero when perpendicular.

mistakes.w: The dynamo output is a steady, constant d.c.
mistakes.r: It is d.c. because it never reverses, but it **varies in size**, falling to zero twice per turn.

mistakes.w: Slip rings reverse the current.
mistakes.r: Slip rings **do not** swap connections; the current reverses because the coil sides change direction of movement.

mistakes.w: A generator makes electricity from nothing once it is spinning.
mistakes.r: Work must be done because the induced current produces a force that **opposes the rotation**.

mistakes.w: The commutator makes the current in the coil stop reversing.
mistakes.r: The p.d. in the coil still reverses; the commutator swaps the **connections to the external circuit** so the external current is one way.

exam.q: Name the part that makes an alternator's output a.c. rather than d.c.
model: Slip rings
exam.tip: Spell out 'slip rings', not just 'rings'.

exam.q: State the difference in construction between an alternator and a dynamo.
model: Alternator uses slip rings
Dynamo uses a split-ring commutator
exam.tip: Two clear statements, one for each.

exam.q: Explain why a p.d. is induced across the coil of a generator as it rotates.
model: The coil cuts magnetic field lines / the field through the coil changes
So a p.d. is induced (electromagnetic induction)
exam.tip: The word 'change' or 'cuts' is essential.

exam.q: Sketch a graph of p.d. against time for (a) an alternator and (b) a dynamo.
model: (a) Sine-shaped wave going above and below the time axis
(b) Series of humps all above the axis, touching zero
exam.tip: Keep peak heights and timings the same for both from the same coil.

exam.q: The coil of an alternator is rotated twice as fast. Describe two changes to the p.d.-time graph.
model: Peak p.d. is larger (about double)
Frequency doubles / period halves / waves closer together
exam.tip: Two different effects, two marks.

exam.q: State two changes to an alternator, other than speed, that increase the peak p.d., and say how each affects the frequency.
model: Stronger magnets / stronger field
More turns on the coil (or iron core)
Frequency stays the same for both
exam.tip: Only speed changes the frequency.

exam.q: Explain why the induced p.d. is zero when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field.
model: The sides of the coil are moving parallel to the field lines (at that instant)
So they are not cutting field lines / no change, so no p.d.
exam.tip: Link to rate of cutting.

exam.q: Explain how a split-ring commutator in a dynamo produces a d.c. output.
model: The p.d. induced in the coil reverses every half turn
The commutator swaps the coil's connections to the brushes every half turn
At the same moment, so the current in the external circuit is always in the same direction
exam.tip: Timing is the key idea: both reversals happen together.

exam.q: A cyclist finds the bike is harder to pedal when the dynamo lamp is on. Explain why.
model: A current flows in the dynamo coil when the lamp is on
The current in the magnetic field produces a force / its field opposes the rotation
So more work must be done to turn it; energy is transferred to the lamp
exam.tip: With the lamp off there is no current and no opposing force.

exam.q: An alternator's output has a period of 0.02 s. Calculate the frequency and state the number of rotations per second.
model: 50 rotations per second
exam.tip: One rotation = one cycle for a simple alternator.

exam.q: Describe and explain how an alternator generates alternating current. Include how the output varies during one rotation.
model: Coil rotated in a magnetic field
Sides cut field lines / field through coil changes, so a p.d. is induced
Each side moves up then down, so the p.d. reverses every half turn
Slip rings keep each end connected to the same brush, so the output is a.c.
p.d. is maximum when coil plane is parallel to field (cutting fastest)
p.d. is zero when coil plane is perpendicular to field
One cycle per rotation; graph is a sine-shaped wave
exam.tip: Level 3 needs a full sequence and the variation through one rotation.

worked.q: An alternator coil rotates 25 times per second with a peak p.d. of 6 V. The speed is increased to 50 rotations per second. State the new frequency, period and approximate peak p.d.
steps: Original frequency = 25 Hz, so period = 1 / 25 = 0.04 s
New frequency = 50 rotations per second = 50 Hz
New period T = 1 / f = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s
Rotating twice as fast doubles the rate of change of field, so peak p.d. roughly doubles to about 12 V

worked.q: A student replaces the slip rings of an alternator with a split-ring commutator, keeping everything else the same. Describe the new output graph.
steps: The device is now a dynamo
The commutator swaps the connections every half turn, when the p.d. in the coil reverses
So the negative halves of the a.c. wave are flipped above the axis
Peak p.d. and the time per half turn are unchanged
worked.ans: A row of humps, all positive, same peak and same time per hump: varying d.c.

phy_ocra.9.4.summary: A **transformer** changes the size of an **alternating** potential difference. It has a **primary coil** and a **secondary coil** wound on a shared **iron core**: the alternating current in the primary makes a constantly changing magnetic field in the core, which **induces an alternating p.d.** in the secondary. The ratio of the p.d.s equals the ratio of the turns, **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**, and for a 100% efficient transformer the power in equals the power out, **Vp x Ip = Vs x Is**. Step-up transformers raise the p.d. for the National Grid so the current is small and less energy is wasted heating the cables; step-down transformers lower it again for safe use in homes.

core.p: A transformer is a device that **increases or decreases an alternating potential difference**. It has no moving parts and works only with a.c.
bullets: **Primary coil**: the input coil, connected to the a.c. supply
**Secondary coil**: the output coil, connected to the load
**Iron core**: a soft iron ring that both coils are wound on
The two coils are **not electrically connected**; energy passes between them through the changing magnetic field
Coils are made of insulated wire so current goes round the turns, not through the core

callouts.p: A device made of two coils wound on an iron core that **changes the size of an alternating potential difference** by electromagnetic induction.

core.p: The transformer uses the fact that an alternating current in one coil can induce a current in another coil. Follow the chain step by step.
bullets: An **alternating current** flows in the primary coil
This produces a magnetic field in the iron core that is **constantly changing** in size and direction
The **iron core** concentrates the field and carries it through the secondary coil
The changing magnetic field through the secondary coil **induces an alternating p.d.** across it
If the secondary is connected to a circuit, an alternating current flows in it

callouts.p: A p.d. is only induced in the secondary while the magnetic field is **changing**. a.c. changes all the time, so it induces a p.d. all the time.

core.h: Why transformers do not work with d.c.
core.p: A steady direct current produces a steady magnetic field in the core. A steady field is not changing, so no p.d. is induced in the secondary coil.
bullets: d.c. in primary gives a **constant** magnetic field
No change in field means **no induced p.d.** in the secondary
There may be a brief pulse at the instant d.c. is switched on or off, as the field changes
This is one reason mains electricity is supplied as a.c.

callouts.p: Do not say 'a transformer works with d.c. but less well'. With steady d.c. the output is **zero**.

core.p: The core is made of **soft iron**, which is easily magnetised and demagnetised. This lets the field build up and reverse quickly as the a.c. alternates.
bullets: **Concentrates** the magnetic field produced by the primary
**Links** the field to the secondary, so almost all of it passes through the secondary coil
Makes the transformer far more efficient than two coils in air
Iron is a magnetic material; it is not there to carry current

core.p: The p.d. induced in each turn is the same in both coils, because the same changing field passes through both. So the p.d. across each coil is proportional to its number of turns.
bullets: **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**
Vp = p.d. across the primary coil (V)
Vs = p.d. across the secondary coil (V)
Np = number of turns on the primary coil
Ns = number of turns on the secondary coil
Rearranged: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np
The turns ratio has no units

callouts.p: potential difference across primary / potential difference across secondary = number of turns on primary / number of turns on secondary
More turns on the secondary always means a bigger output p.d. If your answer does not match this, you have flipped the ratio.

core.p: The number of turns on each coil decides whether the p.d. is increased or decreased.
bullets: **Step-up**: Ns greater than Np, so Vs greater than Vp
**Step-down**: Ns less than Np, so Vs less than Vp
If Np = Ns the output p.d. equals the input (an isolating transformer)
Step-up transformers are used at power stations; step-down at substations and in phone chargers

core.p: A transformer cannot create energy. If it is assumed to be **100% efficient**, the power supplied to the primary equals the power delivered by the secondary. Since power = p.d. x current:
bullets: **Vp x Ip = Vs x Is**
Ip and Is are the currents in the primary and secondary (A)
So if the p.d. is stepped up, the current is **stepped down** by the same factor
If the p.d. is stepped down, the current is stepped up
Real transformers are very efficient (often over 95%) but lose a little energy by heating the coils and core

callouts.p: potential difference across primary x current in primary = potential difference across secondary x current in secondary (Vp x Ip = Vs x Is), for a 100% efficient transformer.
Stepping up the p.d. does not give more power. Higher p.d. always comes with lower current.

core.h: Why the National Grid uses high p.d.
core.p: Power stations need to send large amounts of power along cables hundreds of kilometres long. The cables have resistance, so a current heats them and wastes energy. The power wasted as heat is P = I^2 x R, so it depends on the **square of the current**.
bullets: Step-up transformers raise the p.d. to very high values (e.g. **400 000 V**)
For the same power (P = V x I), a higher p.d. means a **much smaller current**
Smaller current means **less heating** of the cables and **less energy wasted**
Halving the current cuts the heating loss to one quarter
This makes the grid more efficient and allows thinner, cheaper cables

callouts.p: Step up p.d., so current is lower (for same power), so less heating in cables, so less energy wasted / more efficient.

core.p: Very high p.d. is extremely dangerous and would need heavy insulation in homes. Step-down transformers at substations reduce the p.d. in stages to make it safe.
bullets: Reduce to about **230 V** for UK homes
Some industry receives higher p.d. (e.g. 11 000 V or 33 000 V)
Small step-down transformers in chargers reduce 230 V to a few volts for phones and laptops
Each step-down increases the current available at the lower p.d.

core.p: Exam questions often need you to use both equations in one problem. Work in a clear order.
bullets: Use Vp / Vs = Np / Ns to find a missing p.d. or number of turns
Then use Vp x Ip = Vs x Is to find a missing current
Or use power = p.d. x current for the input and output power
Always write the equation, substitute, then give the answer with a unit
Check: step-up p.d. means step-down current

callouts.p: Turns have no unit. p.d. in volts, current in amps, power in watts. Convert kV to V before calculating power.

core.p: Real transformers are not quite 100% efficient. Some energy is transferred to the thermal store of the coils and core.
bullets: Coils have resistance, so current heats them
The changing field also heats the iron core slightly
efficiency = useful power output / total power input
Losses are small, so the 100% assumption is good enough for GCSE calculations unless told otherwise

analogy.p: A transformer is like a set of gears. A small gear driving a big gear trades speed for force; a big gear driving a small one trades force for speed, but the work put in equals the work out (ignoring friction). In the same way, a step-up transformer trades current for p.d. and a step-down transformer trades p.d. for current, with power in equal to power out. The turns ratio plays the role of the gear ratio. Where it breaks down: gears are linked by touching teeth, but the two coils never touch; they are linked only by a changing magnetic field, which is why a transformer needs a.c. and stops working with steady d.c.

terms.d: A device with two coils on an iron core that changes the size of an alternating p.d.
The input coil, connected to the a.c. supply.
The output coil, in which an alternating p.d. is induced.
Soft iron on which both coils are wound; it concentrates and links the changing magnetic field.
A transformer with more turns on the secondary than the primary, so the output p.d. is higher.
A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary than the primary, so the output p.d. is lower.
Np / Ns, the ratio of primary turns to secondary turns; equal to Vp / Vs.
Current that repeatedly reverses direction, producing a changing magnetic field.
Inducing a p.d. across a conductor by changing the magnetic field around it.
The network of cables and transformers that connects power stations to consumers across the UK.
Rate of energy transfer; for electrical circuits, power = p.d. x current, in watts (W).
An ideal transformer with no energy losses, so Vp x Ip = Vs x Is.
A site where step-down transformers reduce the p.d. from the transmission cables.
Energy wasted as cables heat up because of their resistance; depends on the current squared.

mistakes.w: Transformers work with d.c.
mistakes.r: Transformers need **a.c.**: a steady d.c. gives a steady field, so **no p.d. is induced** in the secondary.

mistakes.w: Current flows through the iron core from one coil to the other.
mistakes.r: The coils are not electrically connected; the **changing magnetic field** in the core induces the p.d. in the secondary.

mistakes.w: High voltage reduces resistance in the cables.
mistakes.r: High p.d. means **lower current** for the same power, so **less heating** (energy loss); resistance is unchanged.

mistakes.w: A step-up transformer increases the power.
mistakes.r: Power in = power out (ideal); a higher p.d. comes with a **lower current**.

mistakes.w: Writing Vp / Vs = Ns / Np.
mistakes.r: The correct ratio is **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**: more secondary turns gives more secondary p.d.

mistakes.w: The iron core is there to conduct electricity.
mistakes.r: The iron core **concentrates/links the magnetic field** between the coils.

mistakes.w: High voltage is used because it travels faster.
mistakes.r: It is used to **reduce the current**, so less energy is wasted heating the cables.

mistakes.w: A step-down transformer reduces the current too.
mistakes.r: A step-down transformer **increases** the current (Vp x Ip = Vs x Is).

exam.q: State the purpose of a transformer.
model: To change (increase or decrease) the size of an alternating p.d.
exam.tip: Include 'alternating'.

exam.q: State what is meant by a step-down transformer.
model: Output (secondary) p.d. is smaller than the input (primary) p.d.
Fewer turns on the secondary coil than the primary coil
exam.tip: Give both the p.d. and turns ideas.

exam.q: A transformer has 400 turns on the primary and 20 turns on the secondary. The primary p.d. is 230 V. Calculate the secondary p.d.
model: Vs = Vp x Ns / Np = 230 x 20 / 400
exam.tip: Fewer secondary turns, so expect a smaller answer.

exam.q: Explain why a transformer will not work if the primary coil is connected to a battery.
model: A battery gives d.c., which produces a steady/unchanging magnetic field
No change in field so no p.d. is induced in the secondary
exam.tip: Use the word 'change'.

exam.q: Explain how an alternating current in the primary coil produces a p.d. across the secondary coil.
model: a.c. in primary produces a changing magnetic field
The iron core concentrates/carries the field to the secondary coil
The magnetic field through the secondary is changing
So an alternating p.d. is induced across the secondary (electromagnetic induction)
exam.tip: Each step of the chain is one mark.

exam.q: A step-up transformer changes 25 000 V to 400 000 V. The current in the primary is 800 A. Assuming it is 100% efficient, calculate the current in the secondary.
model: Vp x Ip = Vs x Is
Is = 50 A
exam.tip: Stepping up p.d. by 16 times steps the current down by 16 times.

exam.q: Explain why electricity is transmitted across the National Grid at a very high p.d.
model: For the same power, a high p.d. means a low current
A lower current causes less heating in the cables
So less energy is wasted / transmission is more efficient
exam.tip: Do not say it reduces resistance.

exam.q: Explain why step-down transformers are needed before electricity reaches homes.
model: The very high p.d. of the grid would be dangerous
Step-down transformers reduce it to about 230 V, which is safer to use
exam.tip: Quote 230 V for UK mains.

exam.q: A transformer has 50 turns on its primary coil. It is designed to step up 12 V to 240 V. Calculate the number of turns on the secondary.
model: Ns = Np x Vs / Vp = 50 x 240 / 12
Ns = 1000 turns
exam.tip: No unit for turns.

exam.q: Explain the structure and operation of a transformer, and explain how step-up and step-down transformers are used in the National Grid to reduce energy losses.
model: Primary and secondary coils wound on an iron core
a.c. in primary produces a changing magnetic field in the core
Changing field induces an alternating p.d. in the secondary
Vp / Vs = Np / Ns: more turns on secondary steps up the p.d.
Step-up transformers at power station increase p.d., so current decreases (Vp Ip = Vs Is)
Lower current means less heating of cables, so less energy wasted
Step-down transformers reduce p.d. to safe 230 V for homes
exam.tip: Level 3: explain operation AND link high p.d. to low current to less heating.

worked.q: A phone charger contains a transformer that steps 230 V down to 5 V. The primary coil has 2300 turns. How many turns are on the secondary?
steps: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns
Ns = 50 turns

worked.q: A power station generates 20 MW at 25 kV. A step-up transformer raises this to 400 kV. Assuming 100% efficiency, find the current before and after the transformer.
steps: Power = p.d. x current, so I = P / V
After: Vp x Ip = Vs x Is gives Is = 25 000 x 800 / 400 000
Is = 50 A
worked.ans: 800 A before, 50 A after: the current is 16 times smaller.

worked.q: Using the result above, compare the heating loss in a cable of resistance 5 ohms at 800 A and at 50 A.
steps: Power loss = I^2 x R
Loss is 256 times smaller (16^2)
worked.ans: 3.2 MW versus 12.5 kW: stepping up the p.d. cuts heating losses dramatically.
