phy_ocra.9.5.summary: Microphones and loudspeakers are two halves of the same idea. A **loudspeaker** (and headphones) uses the **motor effect**: an alternating current in a coil sitting in a permanent magnet's field feels a force that keeps reversing, so the coil and cone vibrate and push on the air to make sound. A **moving-coil microphone** uses **electromagnetic induction**: the pressure variations in a sound wave make a diaphragm and coil vibrate in a magnetic field, so an alternating potential difference is induced, which drives a varying current in the circuit that copies the sound.

core.p: OCR asks you to explain how a microphone converts the **pressure variations in sound waves** into **variations in current** in an electrical circuit, and how the reverse effect is used in **loudspeakers and headphones**. This is triple (separate) physics content and links P4.2a-c (motor effect) with P4.2e (electromagnetic induction).
bullets: Loudspeaker / headphones: electrical signal in, sound out, works by the **motor effect**.
Microphone: sound in, electrical signal out, works by **electromagnetic induction** (the generator effect).
Both contain a **coil of wire**, a **permanent magnet** and a part that vibrates (a **cone** or a **diaphragm**).
You must be able to describe the sequence of events step by step and explain WHY each step happens.

callouts.p: A loudspeaker turns a varying current into pressure variations in air; a microphone turns pressure variations in air into a varying current. A moving-coil loudspeaker can even work (badly) as a microphone.

core.p: Sound is a **longitudinal wave**: air particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels, creating regions of high pressure (**compressions**) and low pressure (**rarefactions**). Any device that makes sound must push the air back and forth; any device that detects sound must respond to these pressure changes.
bullets: **Frequency** of the sound (pitch) = number of compressions passing per second, measured in Hz.
**Amplitude** of the sound (loudness) = how big the pressure variation is.
Human hearing range is about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
A loudspeaker must vibrate at the same frequency as the sound it makes; a microphone diaphragm vibrates at the same frequency as the sound hitting it.

callouts.p: Write 'pressure variations' or 'compressions and rarefactions' rather than just 'sound hits the microphone'.

core.p: A typical loudspeaker has a cylindrical **permanent magnet** shaped so that there is a strong **radial magnetic field** in a narrow circular gap. A light **coil** (the voice coil) sits in this gap and is fixed to a **paper or plastic cone**. The cone is held at its edge by a flexible suspension so it can move in and out.
bullets: The magnetic field lines cross the coil wire at **right angles** all the way round, so the force on every part of the coil acts in the same direction (in or out).
The coil is connected to an **amplifier**, which supplies an **alternating current** that carries the audio signal.
The cone is large and light so it can push a lot of air and respond quickly to changes in force.
Headphones contain the same parts, just much smaller.

core.p: The loudspeaker uses the **motor effect**: a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. Because the signal is an **alternating current**, the direction of the force keeps reversing, which makes the coil and cone vibrate.
bullets: 1. An **alternating current** from the amplifier flows through the coil.
2. The coil is in the magnetic field of the permanent magnet, so it experiences a **force** (motor effect).
3. When the current reverses direction, the **force reverses direction** (Fleming's left-hand rule).
4. So the coil moves in and out, and the cone attached to it **vibrates**.
5. The vibrating cone pushes and pulls on the air, producing **compressions and rarefactions**: a sound wave.
6. The cone vibrates at the **same frequency as the alternating current**, so the sound has that frequency.

callouts.p: Frequency of sound produced = frequency of the alternating current in the coil.

core.h: Loudness, pitch and the size of the force
core.p: The force on the coil is given by F = B x I x l (Higher). A bigger current means a bigger force, so the cone moves further each way: a larger amplitude of vibration and a **louder** sound. A higher frequency current makes the cone vibrate more times per second: a **higher pitch**.
bullets: Bigger **current** -> bigger force -> larger amplitude -> louder sound.
Stronger **magnet** (bigger B) -> bigger force for the same current -> louder.
More **turns** on the coil (more length l of wire in the field) -> bigger force.
Higher **frequency** of current -> higher frequency of vibration -> higher pitch.
Real music is a complicated mixture of frequencies; the current copies the whole waveform and the cone copies the current.

head: Change to the current
Effect on cone
Effect on sound
rows: Pushed one way and stays there

callouts.p: A steady direct current gives a steady force, so the cone moves once and stops. Sound needs a current that keeps changing.

core.p: A moving-coil (dynamic) microphone is built like a tiny loudspeaker: a light **diaphragm** is attached to a **coil** that sits in the magnetic field of a **permanent magnet**. The ends of the coil are connected to a circuit, often via an amplifier.
bullets: The diaphragm is very thin and light so that even small pressure variations can move it.
The coil is free to move back and forth in the magnetic field.
The output is a small **alternating potential difference** (p.d.), usually only millivolts, so it is amplified.

core.p: The microphone uses **electromagnetic induction** (the generator effect): when a conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, a **potential difference is induced** across it. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a **current** flows.
bullets: 1. Sound waves (pressure variations) reach the microphone.
2. The changing pressure makes the **diaphragm vibrate** back and forth.
3. The coil attached to the diaphragm **moves in the magnetic field** (it cuts magnetic field lines).
4. A **potential difference is induced** in the coil.
5. As the coil moves one way then the other, the induced p.d. **reverses direction**, so it is an **alternating p.d.**
6. In a complete circuit this drives an **alternating current** whose variations match the pressure variations of the sound.
7. The induced current has the **same frequency** as the sound wave, and a larger amplitude for louder sound.

callouts.p: A potential difference is induced across a conductor when it moves relative to a magnetic field (or when the magnetic field around it changes).

core.h: Why the induced signal copies the sound
core.p: The size of the induced p.d. depends on **how fast** the coil cuts field lines. A louder sound pushes the diaphragm further and faster, so a bigger p.d. is induced. A higher-pitched sound moves the coil back and forth more often, so the p.d. alternates more often.
bullets: Louder sound -> larger diaphragm movement -> faster coil movement -> **larger induced p.d. and current**.
Higher frequency sound -> coil changes direction more often -> **higher frequency** current.
Stronger magnet or more turns on the coil -> larger induced p.d. for the same sound.
The electrical signal is an **analogue** copy of the sound: its shape matches the pressure variations.

callouts.p: Six-mark answers score best when each step is linked with 'so' or 'which causes': sound -> diaphragm vibrates -> coil moves in field -> p.d. induced -> alternating current.

core.p: The two devices have almost identical parts but use opposite physics and convert energy in opposite directions.
bullets: Loudspeaker: **electrical** energy transferred to **kinetic** energy of the cone, then to sound.
Microphone: energy carried by **sound** transferred to kinetic energy of the diaphragm, then **electrically**.
Both rely on relative motion or force between a coil and a permanent magnet's field.

rows: Induced p.d. opposes the change (Lenz, not needed in detail)

callouts.p: Loudspeaker = motor effect. Microphone = induction. Swapping these is the most common way to lose the mark.

core.p: Headphones are small loudspeakers placed next to the ear. They work in exactly the same way: an alternating current in a coil in a magnetic field produces an alternating force, so a small diaphragm vibrates and creates pressure variations in the air in the ear canal.
bullets: Smaller cone/diaphragm and smaller current, because the sound only needs to travel a few millimetres.
Often use strong neodymium magnets so the force is large enough even with a tiny coil.
The spec explicitly names headphones, so mention them when asked about the reverse effect.

core.p: In a public address system the microphone converts sound into a small varying current, an **amplifier** increases its amplitude (supplying energy from the mains or a battery), and the loudspeaker converts the larger varying current back into louder sound.
bullets: Microphone output is tiny, so the amplifier is essential.
The frequency is kept the same at each stage; only the amplitude is increased.
If the loudspeaker is too near the microphone, its sound is picked up again and amplified in a loop, giving a howl (feedback).

callouts.p: Each stage keeps the same frequency and waveform shape so the output sound is a faithful copy of the input sound.

core.h: Linking to F = BIl and induction factors (Higher)
core.p: Higher tier questions may ask you to use F = B x I x l for the force on the loudspeaker coil, where F is force in newtons, B is magnetic flux density in tesla, I is current in amperes and l is the length of wire in the field in metres.
bullets: Length l for a coil = number of turns x circumference of one turn.
Doubling the current doubles the force (F is directly proportional to I).
For a microphone, the induced p.d. increases with the speed of movement, the strength of the field and the number of turns.
Units: 1 T = 1 N/(A m).

callouts.p: Coil lengths are often given in cm and currents in mA. Convert to m and A before using F = BIl.

analogy.p: A loudspeaker is like someone bouncing a trampoline sheet up and down by pulling a rope: the rope tug (the alternating force from the current) moves the sheet (cone), which pushes the air. A microphone is the reverse: someone jumps on the trampoline (sound pressure), and the moving sheet pulls a rope that turns a dynamo (coil in a field) to make electricity. Where it breaks down: there is no physical rope; the force acts through the magnetic field with no contact, and the induced p.d. appears only while the coil is moving, not from its position.

terms.d: A device that converts an alternating electrical current into sound waves using the motor effect.
A device that converts the pressure variations of sound waves into variations in current (an electrical signal) using electromagnetic induction.
A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force.
The induction of a potential difference across a conductor that moves relative to a magnetic field, or that is in a changing magnetic field.
A current that repeatedly reverses its direction.
A p.d. produced across a conductor by electromagnetic induction; it drives a current if the circuit is complete.
A thin, light, flexible sheet in a microphone that vibrates when sound pressure variations hit it.
The light paper or plastic part of a loudspeaker, attached to the coil, that vibrates and pushes the air.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time.
Many turns of insulated wire in the magnet's field; it is attached to the cone or diaphragm.
A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are close together and pressure is higher.
A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are spread out and pressure is lower.
The number of complete vibrations or waves per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The maximum displacement of a vibration from its rest position; for sound, larger amplitude means louder.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).
A device that increases the amplitude of an electrical signal without changing its frequency.

mistakes.w: A loudspeaker works by electromagnetic induction.
mistakes.r: A loudspeaker works by the motor effect: a current in a magnetic field experiences a force.

mistakes.w: A microphone works by the motor effect.
mistakes.r: A microphone works by electromagnetic induction: the coil moves in a magnetic field so a p.d. is induced.

mistakes.w: The magnet vibrates in a loudspeaker.
mistakes.r: The coil and cone vibrate; the permanent magnet is fixed.

mistakes.w: The current in the coil is direct current.
mistakes.r: It is alternating current; the force must keep reversing so the cone vibrates.

mistakes.w: The sound hits the coil and makes electricity.
mistakes.r: Pressure variations make the diaphragm vibrate, which moves the coil in the magnetic field, inducing a p.d.

mistakes.w: A louder sound has a higher frequency current.
mistakes.r: A louder sound gives a larger amplitude current; a higher pitch gives a higher frequency current.

mistakes.w: The microphone produces a current even when the diaphragm is still.
mistakes.r: A p.d. is only induced while the coil is moving relative to the field.

mistakes.w: The coil is attracted to the magnet like an electromagnet picking up iron.
mistakes.r: The force is the motor effect: the interaction between the field of the current and the field of the permanent magnet, reversing with the current.

exam.q: State the effect used by a loudspeaker to produce sound.
model: The motor effect (a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force).
exam.tip: One mark: name the effect precisely.

exam.q: State the effect used by a moving-coil microphone.
model: Electromagnetic induction (generator effect).
exam.tip: Do not write 'motor effect' here.

exam.q: Explain why a loudspeaker must be supplied with an alternating current rather than a direct current.
model: The force on the coil reverses direction each time the current reverses.
So the cone vibrates back and forth, producing sound; d.c. would give a steady force with no vibration.
exam.tip: Link reversing current to reversing force.

exam.q: A loudspeaker is connected to a signal generator. Describe what happens to the sound when the frequency of the a.c. is increased.
model: The cone vibrates more times per second / at a higher frequency.
So the pitch of the sound increases.
exam.tip: Frequency of sound = frequency of current.

exam.q: Suggest two ways the loudness of a loudspeaker could be increased without changing the amplifier.
model: Use a stronger permanent magnet.
Use more turns of wire on the coil (greater length of wire in the field).
exam.tip: Think of the factors in F = BIl.

exam.q: Explain how a moving-coil microphone converts sound into an electrical signal.
model: Pressure variations / compressions and rarefactions of the sound make the diaphragm vibrate.
The coil attached to the diaphragm moves in the magnetic field of the permanent magnet.
A potential difference is induced in the coil.
The p.d. alternates as the coil moves back and forth, giving an alternating current with the same frequency as the sound.
exam.tip: Use the word 'induced'.

exam.q: Explain how a loudspeaker converts an electrical signal into sound.
model: An alternating current flows in the coil, which is in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet.
The coil experiences a force (motor effect).
The force reverses as the current reverses, so the coil and cone vibrate.
The cone produces pressure variations (compressions and rarefactions) in the air: a sound wave.
exam.tip: Name the cone and the air pressure variations.

exam.q: A student says a microphone and a loudspeaker are the same device used in reverse. Evaluate this statement.
model: Both have a coil, a permanent magnet and a vibrating part (cone or diaphragm).
A loudspeaker uses the motor effect to turn current into motion and sound.
A microphone uses electromagnetic induction to turn motion caused by sound into a p.d./current.
So the structure is similar but the physics and energy transfer are opposite; a speaker can act as a crude microphone, so the statement is largely correct.
exam.tip: Evaluate means give both sides and a conclusion.

exam.q: The coil of a loudspeaker has a length of 4.0 m of wire in a field of 0.80 T. Calculate the maximum force on the coil when the current is 0.50 A.
exam.tip: Higher only. Check units are T, A and m.

exam.q: A singer uses a microphone connected through an amplifier to a loudspeaker. Explain, in detail, how the singer's voice is reproduced louder by the loudspeaker.
model: Sound waves from the voice are pressure variations that make the microphone diaphragm vibrate.
The coil attached to it moves in a magnetic field so an alternating p.d. is induced (electromagnetic induction).
This produces a small alternating current with the same frequency and waveform as the sound.
The amplifier increases the amplitude of the current but keeps the frequency the same.
In the loudspeaker, the alternating current in the coil in a magnetic field gives an alternating force (motor effect), so the cone vibrates.
The cone vibrates with a larger amplitude, producing compressions and rarefactions in the air: the same sound but louder.
exam.tip: Level of response: cover both devices, name both effects, and mention frequency staying the same.

worked.q: A loudspeaker coil has 50 turns, each of circumference 0.060 m. It sits in a radial field of 0.50 T. Calculate the force on the coil when the current is 0.20 A.
steps: Length of wire in field: l = 50 x 0.060 = 3.0 m.
Use F = B x I x l.
worked.ans: 0.30 N (the direction reverses every time the a.c. reverses).

worked.q: The current in the coil in the previous example is doubled and its frequency changed from 256 Hz to 512 Hz. Describe and explain the change in the sound.
steps: Doubling I doubles F (F = BIl), so the force becomes 0.60 N.
A bigger force moves the cone further, so the amplitude of vibration increases: louder sound.
The frequency of the a.c. doubles, so the cone vibrates twice as many times per second.
Frequency of sound equals frequency of current, so the sound is 512 Hz: a higher pitch (one octave higher).
worked.ans: The sound becomes louder and higher in pitch (512 Hz).

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a moving-coil microphone gives no output in a silent room even though it contains a magnet and a coil.
steps: Electromagnetic induction needs relative motion between the coil and the magnetic field.
In silence there are no pressure variations, so the diaphragm does not move.
The coil is stationary in a steady field, so no field lines are cut.
Therefore no p.d. is induced and no current flows.
worked.ans: No sound means no movement of the coil, so no p.d. is induced.
